# Regression - Pre-reading {.unnumbered} Complete this material before your workshop session. It carries the vocabulary you will need in the room. ## Video: from two groups to a line {#sec-video} ::: {.callout-note} ## Watch before class {{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/aFDOzpTeg0s?si=KZvj853cmcHhfGA- >}} After watching, you should be able to explain what the slope of a regression line measures when the predictor is a measurement rather than a group label. ::: ## Learning outcomes {#sec-outcomes} **By the end of this week you should be able to:** 1. interpret the slope of a regression line as the change in the response for a one-unit increase in the predictor, in the units of the data; 2. calculate a fitted value and a residual by hand; 3. explain why least squares uses squared residuals to choose a line; 4. interpret the intercept, and explain how centring the predictor makes it meaningful; 5. use a residual plot to judge whether a straight line describes the data adequately; 6. choose between a confidence interval and a prediction interval, and recognise when a prediction is an extrapolation. ## Reading: fitting a straight line {#sec-reading} ### From two groups to a measurement {#sec-groups-to-measurement} In Session 4 you coded Darwin's two groups as x = 0 (Cross) and x = 1 (Self) and drew a line between their means. The intercept was the mean of the reference group, and the slope, −2.62 inches, was the difference between the two means. That x-axis was a label: no plant sits halfway between cross- and self-pollinated. In **regression**, the predictor is a measurement. Every value between the observed ones means something, so the line describes how the response changes across the whole range of the predictor. The slope is now the change in the response for a **one-unit increase** in the predictor. The model is fitted with the same function, and its output has the same coefficient table: ```r lm(hardness ~ dens, data = janka) ``` The response goes on the left of the `~` and the predictor on the right. The row labelled `(Intercept)` is the intercept, and the row labelled `dens` is the slope. ### The data {#sec-janka} The workshop uses 36 samples of Australian timber. For each sample we have its **density** and its **hardness** on the Janka scale: the force needed to push a steel ball 0.444 inches in diameter halfway into the wood. Density is easy to measure; hardness needs a testing machine. The practical question is whether density can be used to predict hardness. ### The equation of a line {#sec-line} A straight line is described by two numbers: $$ \hat{y} = a + bx $$ - $a$, the **intercept**, is the value of the line at x = 0. - $b$, the **slope**, is the change in y for each one-unit increase in x. - $\hat{y}$ ("y-hat") is the **fitted value**: the value of y that the line predicts for a given x. For example, if a = 2 and b = 0.5, then at x = 10 the line predicts $\hat{y} = 2 + 0.5 \times 10 = 7$. The slope is measured in units of y per unit of x, so its units depend on how the variables were measured. ### Residuals {#sec-residuals} Real data do not lie exactly on a line. The **residual** for each observation is the vertical distance between the observed value and the line: $$ e = y - \hat{y} $$ A point above the line has a positive residual and a point below it has a negative one. Continuing the example, if the observed value at x = 10 is 8, the residual is 8 − 7 = 1. You can draw many different straight lines through the same points, and each gives a different set of residuals. In the workshop you will draw your own line through 8 timber samples, calculate its residuals, and work out with your partner how to decide whose line is best. ### What the coefficient table reports {#sec-coef-table} The coefficient table has the same columns as in Session 4: estimate, standard error, t value and p-value. For the slope, t is still the estimate divided by its standard error, and the p-value tests whether the slope differs from zero. One thing changes: a straight line estimates two coefficients, the intercept and the slope, so the degrees of freedom are the number of observations minus 2. ### Predicting from a line {#sec-predicting} Once you have a line, you can predict y for any value of x. The data only tell you about the range of x that was measured, though. A prediction for a value of x outside that range is called **extrapolation**, and it is much less trustworthy: the line has been extended into a region where there are no observations to support it. ## Commitment task {#sec-commitment} ::: {.callout-warning} ## Bring this to class Two people draw different straight lines through the same scatter of points. Write one or two sentences on how you would decide which line is better. Do not look this up. There is no mark for this and no correct answer is expected; the point is to have something concrete to revise in the workshop. Bring what you wrote to the session, together with a calculator, a pencil and a ruler. ::: ## Self-test {#sec-selftest} ::: {.webex-check .webex-box} **1.** In `lm(height ~ type)` from Session 4, the slope was the difference between two group means. In `lm(hardness ~ dens)`, the slope is: ::: {.cell} :::
**2.** A line has a = 2 and b = 0.5. The fitted value at x = 10 is . **3.** On the same line, the observed value at x = 10 is 5.5. The residual is .
The residual is observed minus fitted: 5.5 − 7 = −1.5. It is negative because the point lies below the line.
**4.** A point lies above the line. Its residual is . **5.** A regression of hardness on density gives an intercept of −1160. Why can an intercept be a value that no real timber could have? ::: {.cell} :::
The intercept is the height of the line at x = 0. No timber has a density near zero, so the line is being extended far beyond the data, where it can produce impossible values. The intercept is still needed to position the line. In the workshop you will see how centring the predictor gives an intercept you can interpret.
**6.** A straight-line regression is fitted to 20 observations. The residual degrees of freedom are . **7.** The Janka data cover densities from 24.7 to 69.1. A prediction for a density of 90 is .
A density of 90 is above the highest density measured, so the model has no observations there to support the prediction.
